q0183: Purple team = red (attack) and blue (defense) working together and sharing findings. White referees; yellow builds the systems.
q0184: Estimated hours, deliverables and cost for one specific engagement = SOW.
q0185: An unexpected login with a built-in admin account = default credentials. Change default passwords at installation.
q0186: Compare the yearly cost of a risk with the yearly cost of insuring against it = ALE (SLE × ARO).
q0187: A legitimate process suddenly doing things it never does (network traffic, spawning shells) = code injected into its memory.
q0188: Insiders are already in the building: protect the data center with its own access control (badges), not perimeter controls like bollards.
q0189: Access that follows group membership for a job = role-based. The user was never moved to the new team's group, so access still matches the old role.
q0190: Load balancers, redundancy, clustering and UPS units all serve availability.
q0191: Installing a new camera (or wireless access point)? Do a site survey first to decide placement and coverage.
q0192: Services up but unreachable + a sudden surge of traffic = DDoS (the network is saturated).
q0193: Profit = organized crime. Causes = hacktivists. Espionage and geopolitics = nation-states. Revenge or grievance = insiders.
q0194: Finding the host that talks to a C2 server → network and firewall logs show the internal source address of the outbound connections.
q0195: Getting past doors, badges and guards = a physical penetration test.
q0196: The same key on both ends = symmetric (AES). A public/private key pair = asymmetric (RSA, ECC).
q0197: Stop strangers plugging into wall jacks = port security (MAC limits or 802.1X), or disable unused ports.
q0198: Reissuing a device: sanitize the old data, then document it (certification). Destruction is for devices leaving service for good.
q0199: How to undo a change if it goes wrong = the backout (rollback) plan.
q0200: Fewer physical servers = virtualization (consolidating many VMs onto each host).
q0201: Detect changes to sensitive files = FIM (hashes compared against a baseline).
q0202: A BIA finds the critical processes and sets RTO, RPO and MTD. Plans and procedures come afterward, built to meet those targets.
q0203: Whether you can fix a CVE depends first on whether a patch exists. No patch → compensating controls.
q0204: Effective change management: approval before the change, testing, a backout plan and documentation. No bypasses.
q0205: A protocol hiding on the wrong port (HTTP over port 53) → NGFW application inspection identifies the real application.
q0206: Encrypt everything that crosses between two networks = an IPSec site-to-site VPN.
q0207: Fingerprinting sensitive files and alerting when they are emailed out = DLP.
q0208: Publish hashes so users can check downloads were not corrupted or tampered with. Code signing adds proof of who published them.
q0209: Protect stored passwords by hashing them (with salts). A stolen hash database does not reveal the passwords directly.
q0210: The same message on every machine + files renamed with a new extension (.ryk) = ransomware (Ryuk).
q0211: Many different source IPs, the same instant, SYN packets to one server = DDoS (SYN flood).
q0212: Time to fix = MTTR. Time between failures = MTBF. Target downtime = RTO. Target data loss = RPO.
